title: A curve for each role of a motion
when: Whenever something arrives, leaves, counts, drifts or the camera moves in a shot.
summary: Human-made motion films never use one easing for everything: landings decelerate hard, leavings accelerate, counters step, drifts are linear. One global ease is the clearest sign of machine-made motion.
do: Landings ease out: about 60-72% of the travel in the first 4-5 frames, then a 0.4-0.6 s tail.
Leavings ease in and are quicker than the arrival; the next thing may enter about 2 frames before the old one is gone.
Camera reframes are a fast snap followed by a slow decelerating tail, never one even tween.
Overshoot is rare and small (under 9% of moves, about +4-8%, late in the move); one big springy payoff per video at most.
Keep one motion grammar per video: crisp steps or smeared fast moves, not both.
avoid: the same ease and duration on every element
a bounce on every pop
exits that are the entrance played backwards

title: Arrive from oversize, never from nothing
when: When a word, number, logo or object first appears.
summary: A thing that lands from a little too big and soft, settling to its size, reads as weight and confidence; growing from zero reads as a toy.
do: Let important things land oversized (1.4-1.6x) and blurred, settling to size in about 0.4 s (enter "land").
A logo or a name may start large and shrink about its own centre.
avoid: scaling up from zero
fading a hero in by opacity alone

title: Words land on the voice
when: When on-screen words build while the narrator speaks.
summary: Words appear whole, on the spoken word, at the speech rhythm; the gap before the key word is longer, which is the emphasis.
do: Cue each on-screen word to the word that speaks it ("at"), landing 0-2 frames ahead of the voice.
Gaps of 3-5 frames between words, a longer gap (about 10 frames) before the key word.
Show the one or two words that matter, not the sentence the voice already says.
avoid: letter-by-letter typing for headlines (typing belongs inside a screen or prompt)
words arriving on a metronome
the whole sentence on screen

title: No frozen frame
when: When a shot holds for reading or for a payoff.
summary: Real holds are alive: something drifts, breathes or creeps. A true stillness is earned after a payoff, or chosen as a breath before one.
do: Keep one living thing on every held frame (a slow drift, a creeping camera of 2-5%, a pulse, a counter settling).
Hold still only after a payoff (0.5-1.0 s) or as a stated breath before it (0.6-1.5 s).
avoid: a static card held for more than a second
a hold-and-swap rhythm where each card sits 1.2 s and is replaced
checks: No frame sequence longer than about 3 flat frames without change, except a stated breath.

title: Numbers roll and land
when: When a number counts up or resolves on screen.
summary: A counter that shows one value per frame with shrinking steps lands like a real readout; a smooth tween reads as a slider.
do: Use a counter (text style counter, gauge, ruler reading) with 15-23 visible steps over 0.5-0.9 s, landing on the narrated value with a small pop.
A claim may land on a round number; measured data lands on its real, un-round value.
avoid: inventing a number the narration does not say
a counter that keeps moving after the voice has said it

title: One accent, one meaning
when: When choosing which element gets the accent colour.
summary: The accent becomes meaning only if it is spent on one role: the hero, the verdict, or the measured reading. Spent everywhere, it means nothing.
do: Give the accent to one role for the whole video (the hero, the key number, the verdict) and mark it accent: true.
A new key word may flash the accent on arrival and settle back to ink after 0.13-0.28 s.
In a film look, the accent is what keeps its colour: put it on the hero.
avoid: two different things in the accent at once
accent used as decoration or a background wash
colour on the same colour (red on red)

title: Cut on motion and carry an object
when: When moving from one shot or scene to the next.
summary: The joins viewers do not notice share something: the last frame of one shot and the first of the next hold the same object, word, ground or position, and both are mid-motion.
do: Carry one object, word or shape across a cut where you can (the coin becomes the planet, the map pin becomes the city).
Cut while things move, and let the next thing enter along the same direction.
After a whip, give 2-3 empty frames before the next element sweeps in.
avoid: default crossfades between unrelated shots
a cut on a dead, settled frame
fading the video to black at the end by default

title: Every cue in the script gets a visual
when: While planning shots from the narration.
summary: Mark the words that need a picture: numbers, abstract nouns, names and contrast words. Each gets a visual built for it; the rest of the sentence the voice carries alone.
do: Numbers: a visual built from the number itself (a counter, a gauge, a unit chart, a ruler, a chart), never just a caption.
Abstract nouns: a concrete metaphor, each metaphor used once per video.
Names (people, places, products): a beat with its own hold (a quote card, a pin, a portrait).
Contrast words (but, instead, not anymore): a turn - a change of ground, colour, scale or camera.
Mute test: with the sound off the pictures still tell the story; with the picture off nothing important is missing from the voice.
avoid: showing the whole sentence as text
a generic picture that matches no cue

title: Concrete pictures for abstract words
when: When a line names an idea that has no object: attention, scale, rarity, sameness, time pressure.
summary: Ask what the word looks like, or what it is the opposite of, and draw that; take props from the audience's own world, not from clip-art.
do: "top 1%": 100 identical people, all dim but one lit in the accent (unit chart).
"commoditised": many identical things flooding in; "different": one standing apart.
"over a weekend": a calendar whose last two days light up.
"billion-dollar": the word three to four times bigger than everything else, alone.
A process that "thinks": an object from the customer's world working, never a glowing orb.
avoid: rockets for launch, shields for security, light bulbs for ideas
the first association of a name (fire for a name that means fire)
reusing one metaphor twice in a video

title: Spend emphasis on few beats
when: When deciding how big each beat should be.
summary: If everything is a peak nothing is. Give each beat an importance and a reason it exists for the viewer.
do: At most a quarter of beats get the biggest treatment (a paid picture, a slam, a full-frame number).
For each beat be able to say what it buys the viewer ("the viewer now sees why the price fell").
Cut beats that buy nothing.

title: Shape the energy of the whole video
when: When pacing shots across a section or the whole video.
summary: Human edits shorten their beats toward a peak placed at 60-75% of the piece, then let the last beat linger.
do: Let shots get shorter as a section builds to its turn (for example 1.3, 1.1, 0.7, 0.45 s), then hold the landing.
Place the strongest moment of each chapter around 60-75% of it.
Give the viewer at least one breath (a held, quiet shot) before the main reveal.
avoid: every beat the same length
the peak in the first or last seconds of a chapter

title: What makes motion look machine-made
when: Before approving a plan or a render.
summary: A list of the habits that make generated videos look like slides or templates, each with the decision a designer would make instead.
avoid: corner chrome: a label, counter or brand line repeated in a corner
deck layouts: a headline top-left with a grey sub-line
a flat colour card per scene with a centred number and a small label (a stat slide)
the same layout at the same place three shots in a row
a new effect on every shot with nothing in common
big faint words or grid lines as decoration behind everything
labels that only name the scene
everything fading in and out
checks: No frame that would read as a presentation slide.
Neighbouring shots share a motif, colour or object and differ in layout.

title: Transitions made of the picture
when: When a scene change needs more than a cut.
summary: Good transitions are made of what is on screen: an object becomes the next ground, a shape fills the frame, the camera dives through a detail.
do: Carried object: the same thing in the same place across the cut.
Effect becomes ground: a growing shape, ink or light fills the frame and is the next background.
Scale cut: from the whole to a detail (or back) on a hard cut.
Mask through a shape or a word into the next scene.
A fast montage only for "many": several looks in quick hard cuts.
avoid: a dissolve between unrelated pictures
a white flash at full strength (cap it near half)

title: Type set by a director
summary: Hierarchy comes from scale, not boldness; words arrive whole on the speech; the key word acts out its meaning; survivors never jump to re-centre.
do: Statements at about 7-11% of frame height, hero figures at 22-29%.
Highlight a key word with a hard box, a hand-drawn loop or a target ring.
Hold text long enough to read it: at least 0.45 s, about 0.2 s per word, 1.7-2.0 s for 6-8 words.
avoid: a serif italic word inside a sans line as the accent
tracked capitals taglines
a giant single word alone on a flat ground as a slide
